Operator:
Good day, and welcome to the MediCore Devices Third Quarter Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your telephone. Please note, this call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call will contain forward-looking statements, including expectations regarding our future performance, business outlook, and financial results. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Joining me on today's call are Alex Rivera, CEO; Mike Chen, CFO; Dr. Lena Patel, Chief Technology Officer; and Tom Hargrove, Chief Commercial Officer.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. MediCore Devices delivered strong results this quarter, driven by increasing adoption of our innovative medical devices and strategic partnerships.

Today, I will cover five key aspects of our performance. First, capital equipment versus consumables mix trends; second, gross margin trends and supply chain commentary; third, organic revenue growth by segment and geography; fourth, key assumptions underlying the guidance; and fifth, FDA approvals and CE marks obtained.

Mike will then provide a more detailed review of our financials. After that, we'll open the call for your questions.

Now, let's get started with our capital equipment versus consumables revenue mix—a key metric that underscores the annuity-like stability of our business model and our progress toward sustainable, high-margin growth. For those less familiar, capital equipment includes our high-value installed base assets like the CoreScan 4K imaging systems, EchoFlex ultrasound platforms, and our flagship PrecisionNav robotic-assisted surgery suites, similar to Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci ecosystem. Consumables encompass our razor-blade recurring revenues from single-use catheters, disposable end-effectors, guidewires, bio-absorbable stents, and procedure kits—generating predictable streams tied to procedure volumes and our growing installed base.

In Q3, our overall revenue mix stood at 28% capital equipment and 72% consumables, up from 32% capital and 68% consumables in the prior-year period. This represents a 400 basis point shift toward consumables year-over-year, driving our gross margins to 68.2%—a 210 basis points expansion—and bolstering adjusted EBITDA margins to 32.4%. On a trailing twelve-month basis, consumables now account for 71% of total revenues, up from 65% two years ago, reflecting the maturity of our razor-blade strategy amid hospital budget constraints and a pivot to value-based care.

Let me break this down by key drivers and segments. Capital equipment revenues came in at $285 million, down 8% year-over-year on a constant-currency basis, primarily due to elongated sales cycles for our $2.5 million-plus PrecisionNav systems amid U.S. hospital capex scrutiny following COVID supply chain normalization. Average selling prices held steady at $1.8 million per unit, but unit volumes dipped 12% to 145 placements, as customers prioritized software upgrades over new installs. Notably, our utilization rates on the installed base improved to 78% from 72% year-over-year, fueled by our NavAI predictive analytics module, which optimizes surgical scheduling and has seen 65% attach rates on new systems.

Consumables, however, were the standout, surging 15% to $735 million, or 22% on an organic basis. This was propelled by an 18% increase in procedure volumes across our cardiology and neurovascular franchises, where single-use devices like our FlexiFlow aspiration catheters—now the market leader with 24% share per the latest Millennium Research report—benefited from expanded indications for stroke thrombectomy. Our installed base grew 11% to 4,200 systems globally, generating $175,000 average annual consumables per box, up 7% due to higher kit complexity and premium pricing on antimicrobial-coated variants amid rising hospital-acquired infection concerns.

Regionally, the trends vary but align with our strategic focus. In the U.S., which represents 52% of revenues, the consumables mix hit 75%, up from 69% year-over-year, driven by CMS reimbursement tailwinds for outpatient ASC procedures under the 2024 OPPS final rule. We saw 20% growth in neuro consumables here, outpacing peers like Penumbra amid the stroke volume boom from aging demographics. EMEA, at 28% of revenues, showed a 68% consumables mix—steady but with capital softening to 25% due to German DRG pressures and UK NHS backlogs; however, our CE Mark for the next-gen EchoFlex PRO has catalyzed a 14% consumables ramp in minimally invasive echo procedures. APAC, our fastest-growing region at 20% of revenues, flipped to a 65% consumables mix from 58%, thanks to China NMPA approvals for PrecisionNav and a 25% installed base expansion in Japan and India, where high procedure growth offsets lower ASPs.

Strategically, we're accelerating this favorable mix shift through three initiatives. First, our Consumables-First platform roadmap, including the Q4 launch of single-use robotic end-effectors for PrecisionNav, projected to boost attach rates to 85% and add $120 million in incremental recurring revenue in FY25. Second, digital ecosystem enhancements like our CoreLink cloud platform, which integrates AI-driven inventory management—similar to Stryker's Mako ecosystem—driving 10-15% utilization uplifts and reducing capital refresh cycles from 7 to 5 years. Third, targeted M&A, such as our recent $450 million acquisition of NeuroCath Dynamics, which brings proprietary guidewires with 30% higher deliverability, immediately accretive to consumables margins by 300 basis points.

Looking forward, we expect the consumables mix to reach 74-76% by year-end, with Q4 capital moderating to 26% amid seasonal installs but consumables growing 18-20%. This positions us resiliently against macro headwinds like inflation in raw materials for nitinol-based devices, while capitalizing on tailwinds like the $15 billion global robotics market CAGR through 2028, per Grand View Research. Our 85% customer retention on consumables underscores the stickiness—once a hospital adopts our ecosystem, lifetime value exceeds $5 million per account.

Now, let's talk about gross margin trends and supply chain commentary. Starting with the headline: for the third quarter, we delivered a consolidated gross margin of 65.2%, up 110 basis points year-over-year from 64.1% and 40 basis points sequentially from Q2's 64.8%. This marks our eighth consecutive quarter of gross margin expansion, bringing our trailing twelve-month margin to 65.0%. On a full-year basis, we're tracking toward the high end of our original guidance range of 64.5% to 65.5%, and we're now raising that to 65.2% to 65.8% to reflect the sustained momentum.

Key drivers included product mix as a tailwind, contributing approximately 80 basis points of expansion. We saw stronger-than-expected uptake in our higher-margin structural heart franchise—particularly our next-gen TAVR valve, the VitalFlow Ultra, which now represents 28% of our cardiology revenue, up from 22% a year ago. This compares favorably to disposables like our legacy catheter lines, which carry mid-50s margins. Similarly, in neuromodulation, our Infinity DBS system benefited from deeper market penetration in the U.S., where we've captured share from competitors like Medtronic's Percept PC, driving mix uplift as elective procedures normalized post-COVID.

Pricing discipline added about 50 basis points. In the U.S., our ASPs held firm at +1.2% year-over-year, supported by our value-based contracting model with the top 15 IDNs, which now covers 45% of our U.S. hospital revenue. We've successfully passed through 60% of inflation via targeted list price increases on our robotic-assisted surgery platforms, akin to Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci model. In Europe, however, pricing pressure from the MDR transition shaved off 20 basis points, as reimbursement delays on our coronary stents under the new EU IVDR regs pushed some volumes into lower-ASP markets.

Offsetting these positives, input cost inflation remains a headwind, pressuring margins by roughly 70 basis points year-over-year. Key culprits include medical-grade resins like PEEK and polycarbonate, up 12% due to sustained petrochemical tightness—echoing the DuPont supply constraints we've all felt industry-wide—and electronic components for our imaging cath lab systems, where semiconductor lead times, though improved to 16 weeks from 30, still carry a 15% premium versus pre-pandemic levels. Freight costs moderated to +8% year-over-year from Q2's double-digit spikes, thanks to our ocean spot rate hedging.

On supply chain dynamics, our multi-year resilience program is yielding tangible results. We've reduced single-source supplier dependency from 28% of our bill of materials in 2021 to just 12% today, with diversification into three qualified vendors for critical titanium alloys used in our orthopedic implants and nitinol for vascular devices. A prime example is our partnership with Carpenter Technology, which has ramped to supply 40% of our shape-memory alloys, mitigating risks from Asian smelter disruptions.

Regionally, North America remains rock-solid, with inventory levels at 7.2 months of supply—down from 8.1 in Q1—allowing us to fulfill 99% of U.S. orders on-time, well ahead of the industry average of 92% per Black Book medtech surveys. In Europe, we've accelerated nearshoring, transferring 25% of our catheter extrusion capacity from China to our new greenfield facility in Monterrey, Mexico, which came online in July. This not only cuts lead times by 40% but also hedges against EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism tariffs starting in 2026. China poses ongoing challenges, with localization mandates now requiring 70% domestic content for Class III devices; we've complied by JV-ing with a Shanghai partner for our electrophysiology mapping systems, but this has capped margins there at 55%, versus 68% globally.

Strategically, we're leaning into technical initiatives to sustain this trajectory. Our Industry 4.0 automation roadmap—$150 million CapEx committed through FY25—includes AI-driven predictive maintenance on our stent crimping lines, which boosted manufacturing throughput by 18% and shaved 2.5% off COGS in Q3. We're also piloting blockchain traceability for our supply chain, integrated with SAP Ariba, to ensure 100% compliance with the U.S. Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act by year-end. Sustainability is another lever: sourcing 35% of our polymers from bio-based alternatives via partnerships with Covestro, which not only future-proofs against ESG regs but also trims volatility tied to fossil fuels.

Looking forward, we see gross margin expansion of 100 to 150 basis points in FY25, driven by further mix shift toward our $2 billion structural heart pipeline—including the FDA-submitted VitalFlow Pro with 4D imaging—and continued productivity gains targeting 300 basis points from automation and procurement. Supply chain risks are contained, with inventories expected to normalize to 6.5 months by Q4, positioning us resiliently amid any macro turbulence, including potential U.S. port strikes or Red Sea reroutings.

Moving on to organic revenue growth by segment and geography. We're particularly pleased to highlight our organic revenue growth, which came in at 9.2% year-over-year, excluding the impacts of foreign exchange and our recent tuck-in acquisition of NeuroVasc Solutions. This marks our fifth consecutive quarter of accelerating organic growth, outpacing the broader medtech industry's estimated 6.8% global growth per our internal tracking aligned with Evaluate MedTech benchmarks.

Starting with our largest segment, Cardiovascular, which represented 42% of total revenue and delivered 12.4% organic growth. This was fueled by a 15% surge in transcatheter aortic valve replacement—or TAVR—procedure volumes in the U.S., as elective cases fully normalized post-COVID backlogs. Our next-gen OmniFlow TAVR platform, with its repositionable design and lower paravalvular leak rates comparable to Edwards Lifesciences' Sapien 3 Ultra, captured an incremental 180 basis points of U.S. market share, reaching 14% per implant tracking data from Millennium Research Group. ASPs held firm at +1.2%, supported by value-based reimbursement wins under CMS's TAVR NCD updates. Internationally, EMEA growth was softer at 8%, tempered by German DRG pressures, but we're mitigating this with our structural heart pipeline, including the upcoming FDA submission for our left atrial appendage closure device in H2.

In Orthopedics, 28% of revenue, we saw robust 11.7% organic growth, driven by hip and knee reconstruction, where volumes grew 13% globally. Our Stryker-inspired Mako robotic-arm integration in our Apex Robotics system drove a 22% increase in robotic-assisted procedures, helping us gain 250 basis points share in the $2.5 billion U.S. robotics market. Cementless implants like our porous titanium-coated stems saw particular strength, with ASPs up 2.5% on premium pricing for outpatient shift enablers amid the ASC boom—ambulatory surgery centers now represent 18% of our ortho mix, up from 12% a year ago. Challenges persist in trauma products, flat at +2%, due to softer hospital budgets, but our strategic focus on biologics augmentation, like BMP-2 alternatives, positions us for 15% growth in H2.

Diagnostics and Monitoring, at 18% of revenue, posted 7.9% organic growth. Here, our AI-powered CardioVue continuous glucose and hemodynamic monitors—akin to Abbott's FreeStyle Libre ecosystem but with wireless ECG integration—drove 20% growth in the wearables sub-segment. U.S. hospital capex recovery post-pandemic supported point-of-care ultrasound sales, up 10%, though ASP erosion of -1% from competitive bundling with Philips and GE HealthCare kept the segment from higher teens. We're countering this with our Q4 launch of a next-gen pulse oximetry platform compliant with FDA's Over-the-Counter clearance pathway, targeting consumer-medtech convergence.

Finally, our MedSurg and Endoscopy segment, 12% of revenue, grew 4.6% organically. Strength in single-use endoscopes, mirroring Boston Scientific's SpyGlass gains, offset headwinds in reusable capital equipment. Procedure volumes in GI were up 6%, but reimbursement cuts in Medicare's APC groupings capped upside. Our initiative to expand our LigaSure-like vessel sealing portfolio into robotic-compatible formats is gaining traction, with early APAC tenders.

Geographically, our U.S. business—65% of revenue—led with 11.8% organic growth, propelled by $1.2 billion in elective procedure tailwinds and our 420 basis points market share expansion across core franchises, per NPNow data. This reflects the full ramp of our commercial team post our Precision 2025 reorganization, which streamlined our 12 direct sales regions.

EMEA, 18% of revenue, grew 6.2%, with strength in the UK and Nordics from NDR wins for our TAVR and robotics lines, but Germany and France lagged at +3% due to INAHTA reassessments and hospital consolidation. We're addressing this via localized manufacturing in Ireland, reducing VAT exposure by 8%.

APAC, 12% of revenue, rebounded sharply to 8.9% growth, led by China at +14% following the resumption of our Class III approvals under the NMPA's accelerated pathway. Our partnerships with Mindray for co-branded diagnostics and robotic training centers in Shanghai drove this, capturing share in the $15 billion Chinese ortho market amid aging demographics. Japan remained steady at +5%, buoyed by our drug-eluting stent relaunch.

Emerging markets like Latin America and Rest of World, 5% of revenue, grew 7.1%, with Brazil's elective procedure normalization and tenders in Mexico for our low-cost ultrasound portfolio.

These results underscore our three-pillar strategy: innovation leadership, with $450 million in R&D yielding 12 FDA 510(k)s this year and a robust Phase I pipeline in neuromodulation; commercial excellence, including digital sales enablement via our VR procedure simulators, boosting rep productivity 18%; and operational resilience, with supply chain diversification reducing single-source risk from 25% to 12% post our Vietnam facility ramp. For Q3, we guide to 9-11% organic growth, with FY24 full-year at 9.5-10.5%, ahead of peers like Intuitive Surgical's projected 12-15% but with superior margins at 68% adjusted gross. Risks include FX volatility and potential U.S. election impacts on IRA medtech provisions, but our 75% recurring revenue mix from service and consumables provides a strong moat.

Next, key assumptions underlying the guidance. Our FY2025 guidance calls for revenue of $2.55 billion to $2.65 billion, representing 12% to 16% reported growth and 13% to 17% organic growth at the midpoint. Adjusted non-GAAP EPS is expected at $4.85 to $5.05, implying 10% to 15% growth. Adjusted gross margin of 68% to 69%, and operating margin expansion of 150 to 250 basis points to 28.5% to 29.5%. These targets reflect a disciplined execution of our Precision Growth 3.0 strategy amid a resilient MedTech backdrop, but they're predicated on several core assumptions across procedures, pricing, mix, regional dynamics, and operational levers.

First, procedure volume growth: the bedrock of our top-line outlook. We assume mid-single-digit global procedure growth of 5% to 7%, weighted heavily toward our core franchises in robotic-assisted surgery, structural heart, and neuromodulation. In RAS—where we hold a 28% installed base share behind Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci Xi/Sp platforms—we project 8% to 10% utilization growth, driven by our Ionix R2 system's expanding adoption in thoracic and colorectal procedures. This mirrors the 9% global RAS procedure uptick we saw in Q4 2024 per our internal tracking, aligned with real-world evidence from the SAGES registry showing a 12% year-over-year increase in soft-tissue robotics.

In structural heart, we assume 6% growth for our TAVR portfolio, akin to Edwards Lifesciences' Sapien 3 trends, buoyed by an aging U.S. population (65+ cohort up 3% year-over-year per Census data) and expanded indications for low-risk patients post-2023 FDA approvals. Neuromodulation, including our next-gen Infinity DBS for Parkinson's, factors in 4% growth, tempered by competition from Medtronic's Percept PC but lifted by 15% penetration in Asia-Pacific epilepsy cases. We explicitly assume no material procedure pull-forwards from elective backlogs, as U.S. hospital capacity utilization stabilizes at 75% per Definitive Healthcare metrics, and we're baking in a 2% normalization for seasonal flu impacts on elective volumes.

Second, pricing and mix dynamics: modest tailwinds with defensive posture. Pricing is assumed flat to up 1% globally, reflecting our value-based pricing model amid payer scrutiny. In the U.S., we project 2% ASP uplift from our Ionix R2 premium consumables (average selling price ~$2,800 per procedure), offset by 1% Medicare sequestration pressure under the 2025 Physician Fee Schedule. Europe assumes flat pricing post-HTA reimbursements for our TAVR Evo platform, similar to Boston Scientific's Acurate neo2 trajectory, with Germany and France contributing 0.5% drag from clawbacks.

Favorable mix adds 2% to organic growth: RAS recurring revenue (75% of segment sales) grows 18% versus 8% for capital systems, driven by a 15% installed base expansion to 4,200 units. We're also assuming a 3-point shift toward higher-margin emerging markets products like our AI-enabled neurostimulators, which boast 72% gross margins versus 65% legacy ortho implants.

Third, regional commentary: U.S. stability, international acceleration. Geographically, we assume U.S. revenue at 62% of total (~$1.6B), growing 11% organically on 7% procedure growth and share gains in integrated delivery networks like Kaiser Permanente. EMEA at 22% (~$570M) assumes 14% growth, fueled by 20% RAS penetration in the UK NHS post-NICE guidance and Italy's PNRR-funded hospital upgrades. APAC, 13% of mix (~$340M), is the accelerant at 22% growth: China JDA approvals for Ionix R2 by Q1F25 drive 30% ramp (mirroring Abbott's Xi'an TAVR hub success), while Japan and India add 15% from bariatric robotics amid 12% obesity prevalence rise per WHO data. Rest of World rounds out at 3%, with LatAm volatility assumed neutral. Foreign exchange is a 1% tailwind, based on current USD/EUR at 1.08 and USD/CNY at 7.2; a 10% USD strengthening would shave 2% off reported growth.

Fourth, margin expansion levers: supply chain resilience and OpEx discipline. Gross margins of 68% to 69% (up 100 bps year-over-year) assume: 150 bps from manufacturing scale on Ionix R2 (Costa Rica facility at 85% utilization vs. 70% today), 50 bps from resin cost deflation (down 8% year-over-year per ICIS indices post-supply chain normalization), offset by 100 bps FX headwind on imported components. No material tariff escalation is baked in, but we're 70% reshored/nearshored versus 50% in 2022.

OpEx grows 10% to $980M (38.5% of revenue), below revenue growth, via AI-driven R&D efficiencies—our CLARA platform now accelerates FDA 510(k) submissions by 25%, targeting three next-gen launches (e.g., RAS vision module with 95% AI tumor detection accuracy). SG&A leverage from digital sales force tools (e.g., VR procedure simulations) caps field rep growth at 5%.

Key enablers include Q1F25 CE Mark for Ionix R2 Gen3 (4K optics, 20% faster docking), positioning us against Stryker's Mako RBT in ortho-RAS hybrids. We're assuming 80% clinical trial enrollment success for our pivotal TAVR trial (n=1,200), with topline data H2F25 unlocking $200M U.S. opportunity. M&A dry powder ($1.2B) targets bolt-ons in electrophysiology, like a tuck-in akin to J&J's Shockwave acquisition. Macro tailwinds: U.S. healthcare spend at 18% GDP per CMS, GLP-1 bariatric synergies boosting RAS by 10%, and hospital capex rebound to $120B per ECGI.

Risks and sensitivities: This guidance assumes no recessionary procedure declines (U.S. GDP +2.1%), stable reimbursement (no DRG rebasing >2%), and supply continuity (no Marburg or avian flu disruptions). Downside: 2% revenue hit from 5% procedure shortfall; upside: 3% from China over-delivery. EPS ±$0.15 per 1% revenue swing. These assumptions are grounded in our proprietary procedure analytics, physician surveys (n=1,500), and cross-checked against peer disclosures from Intuitive, Medtronic, and Abbott. We're confident in delivery but remain agile.

Finally, FDA approvals and CE marks obtained. Before diving deeper into financials, I want to highlight a pivotal milestone for MediCore: our regulatory achievements this quarter, which underscore our leadership in the medical devices space and position us for accelerated growth across key markets. Specifically, we secured two FDA approvals and three CE marks under the stringent EU MDR framework, bringing our total regulatory clearances year-to-date to nine—a 50% increase over the same period last year. These wins not only validate our $250 million R&D investment over the past 24 months but also unlock an estimated $450 million in incremental revenue potential over the next three years, based on our conservative launch models and DCF analyses.

On the FDA front: We received 510(k) clearance for our VitaFlow Gen3 sirolimus-eluting coronary stent system, our next-generation platform building on the success of our VitaFlow Gen2, which already holds a 12% U.S. market share in the drug-eluting stent segment—trailing only Boston Scientific's Synergy and Abbott's Xience families. The Gen3 incorporates our proprietary bioresorbable polymer matrix with 30% thinner struts at 60 microns, reducing neointimal hyperplasia by 25% in our pivotal ORBITER IDE trial (n=1,248 patients, 12-month primary endpoint met with 4.2% TLF rate versus 6.1% for predicate devices; p<0.01). This clearance also earned Breakthrough Device Designation last year, fast-tracking our review by 40%. Launching imminently in the U.S., we project $120 million in peak-year sales by 2027, capturing share from older metallic stents amid rising PCI volumes driven by an aging demographic—U.S. PCI procedures up 8% year-over-year per Premier data.

Our second FDA milestone is even more transformative: full PMA approval for the VitaBeat pulsed-field ablation (PFA) system for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. This is our entry into the booming PFA market, projected to grow at 45% CAGR through 2030 per Grand View Research, as electrophysiologists shift from thermal ablation due to lower complication risks. VitaBeat uses our lattice-tip catheter with adaptive field-shaping algorithms, achieving 92% 1-year freedom from AF in our PULSE pivotal trial (n=785; noninferiority to thermal RF with p=0.002). Compared to Medtronic's PulseSelect or Farapulse from Boston Scientific, our system's single-shot workflow reduces procedure time by 22% to under 90 minutes. U.S. commercial rollout begins Q4, with guided-user-fee timelines ensuring reimbursement under the NTAP pathway—we forecast $180 million in U.S. revenue by FY2026, with gross margins expanding to 78% at scale.

Shifting to Europe: CE marks under MDR—which has certification timelines averaging 18-24 months post-2017 rollout—represent a high bar, especially for Class III devices requiring Notified Body scrutiny from the likes of TÜV Süd or BSI. We obtained full MDR CE marks for three portfolio anchors: VitaFlow Gen3 stent, now cleared for EU launch Q1 2025, aligning with our EuroPCR presentation data showing superior deliverability in calcified lesions (success rate 96.8%); VitaOrtho 3D-printed porous tibial implant for knee revision surgery, leveraging our AI-optimized lattice structures that promote osseointegration 35% faster per DEXA scans in our 2-year IDE-equivalent study, tapping into the EU ortho market growing 7% year-over-year amid rising revision rates (up 12% per EFORT registry); and critically, our VitaSurge endoscopic ultrasound-guided biliary drainage stent, a first-in-class self-expanding fully-covered design with anti-migration barbs, CE-marked for Class IIb under MDR Annex XVI, addressing a $1.2 billion EU TAM for EUS-BD where procedural adoption has surged 28% post-pandemic per ESGE surveys.

Regionally, these clearances diversify our footprint: U.S. approvals drive 65% of our projected incremental revenue, given Medicare reimbursement tailwinds and our 250-salesforce ramp-up. In Europe, CE marks bolster our 22% market share in stents per IQVIA MAT Q3 data, offsetting headwinds from MDR delays that plagued peers like Edwards Lifesciences' Sapien 3 Ultra updates. We're also leveraging these for APAC expansion—our Japan PMDA Shonin for VitaFlow Gen3 is on track for H1 2025, eyeing a $300 million regional opportunity as PCI volumes there grow 10% annually.

Strategically, these aren't isolated wins; they're the fruit of our Regulatory Velocity initiative, which allocated 28% of R&D to parallel FDA-EMA filings and digital twin modeling for predicate bridging—slashing submission cycles by 30%. We've filed four additional PMAs/510(k)s in Q3, including our neuromodulation leadless pacemaker, with 80% on-track for 2025 approvals. Partnerships amplify this: our co-development with Siemens Healthineers on imaging integration for PFA has de-risked adoption, mirroring Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci ecosystem playbook. In summary, these FDA and CE achievements propel MediCore toward our FY2025 guidance of $2.8-3.0 billion in revenue, up 22% at midpoint, with adjusted EBITDA margins expanding 250 basis points to 32%. We're redefining standards in cardio and endo devices amid a $600 billion global market growing at 6.5% CAGR.

I will now turn the call over to Mike Chen for a review of our financial results.

Mike Chen:
Thank you, Alex. As Alex mentioned, we delivered a strong financial performance this quarter. Total revenue reached $1.02 billion, up 12% year-over-year on a reported basis and 14% organically, driven by the consumables strength and regulatory wins Alex outlined. Expenses were well-controlled, with adjusted operating expenses at 36% of revenue, down 50 basis points year-over-year due to scale efficiencies. This led to adjusted EBITDA of $330 million, or 32.4% margin, up from 29.8% last year. GAAP net income was $180 million, or $1.25 per diluted share. Cash flow from operations hit $280 million, supporting $150 million in share repurchases and leaving us with $1.8 billion in liquidity.

For full-year 2024, we're raising revenue guidance to $4.1-4.15 billion, adjusted EPS to $4.20-4.30, reflecting the momentum in mix shift and organic growth. Risks remain around FX and supply, but our balance sheet is fortress-like.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Dr. Lena Patel for an update on our product pipeline.

Dr. Lena Patel:
Thank you, Mike. I'm excited to share some updates on our innovative pipeline. We recently received FDA clearance for the Ionix R2 Gen3 robotic system, a groundbreaking device that promises to revolutionize soft-tissue procedures with 4K optics and 20% faster docking times, building directly on the regulatory successes Alex highlighted like VitaFlow Gen3 and VitaBeat PFA. This expands our RAS portfolio, targeting thoracic and bariatric applications with projected 18% procedure growth.

Beyond that, our structural heart pipeline includes the VitalFlow Pro TAVR with 4D imaging, submitted to FDA and on track for approval next year, alongside neuromodulation advances like the next-gen Infinity DBS with enhanced Asia-Pacific indications. We're also advancing single-use end-effectors for PrecisionNav, set for Q4 launch, and AI-enhanced CardioVue monitors for diagnostics. With 12 new 510(k)s this year and Phase I trials in electrophysiology, our $450 million R&D investment is yielding a $2 billion addressable pipeline, positioning us for 15-20% annual growth in new product revenues.

Now, back to Alex for Q&A.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Lena. Operator, we are now ready to take questions.

Operator:
Thank you. Instructions for asking questions: press star then one. Our first question comes from David Lee with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

David Lee - Goldman Sachs:
Thanks, and congrats on the quarter. Alex, on the capital versus consumables mix, you mentioned the Q4 launch of single-use robotic end-effectors—can you elaborate on the expected attach rates and how that factors into FY25 consumables growth?

Alex Rivera:
Great question, David. The single-use end-effectors for PrecisionNav are a cornerstone of our Consumables-First roadmap. We're projecting attach rates to climb to 85% from current levels, up from 65% on NavAI, as hospitals prioritize infection control and cost-per-procedure optimization. This should layer on $120 million in incremental recurring revenue for FY25, with consumables growth accelerating to 18-20% in Q4 alone. The $450 million NeuroCath acquisition accelerates this further with higher-deliverability guidewires adding 300 basis points to margins right away. It's all about that sticky ecosystem LTV exceeding $5 million per account.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Chen with J.P. Morgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Chen - J.P. Morgan:
Thanks. Mike, on gross margins, with the raise to 65.2-65.8% for the year, how should we think about the offset from input inflation and the automation CapEx play into FY25's 100-150 bps expansion?

Mike Chen:
Emily, spot on. Input inflation, particularly PEEK resins up 12% and semis at 15% premium, headwinded us 70 bps this quarter, but pricing discipline passed through 60% via IDN contracts covering 45% of U.S. revenue. Our Industry 4.0 $150 million CapEx—AI predictive maintenance on stent lines already upped throughput 18%—targets 300 bps productivity in FY25. Nearshoring to Mexico cuts lead times 40%, and bio-based polymers from Covestro hedge volatility. FY25's 68-69% assumes 150 bps from Ionix scale and 50 bps resin deflation, with FX the main offset. Resilient at 70% reshored.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Raj Patel with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Raj Patel - Morgan Stanley:
Good morning. Tom, on organic growth, APAC rebounded nicely to 8.9%—what's driving the China +14% and how does that scale with NMPA approvals?

Tom Hargrove:
Thanks, Raj. China led with +14% post-Class III NMPA resumption, fueled by Mindray co-brands and Shanghai robotic centers capturing ortho share in that $15 billion market amid demographics. Partnerships and training have ramped utilization, with Japan at +5% from stent relaunch. For FY25 guidance, APAC's 22% growth assumes Q1 Ionix R2 JDA, mirroring Abbott's TAVR hubs—China alone 30% ramp. Our Precision 2025 reorg boosted rep productivity 18% via VR sims, and localized Ireland manufacturing cuts EMEA VAT 8%. Emerging LatAm at 7.1% adds diversification.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for that insight, Tom.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Wong with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Lisa Wong - Barclays:
